title: KOSMOS Multi-Slit Data Reduction Pipeline
text:
The KOSMOS Multi-Slit Data Reduction Pipeline is a Python and Jupyter-based tool designed to process spectroscopic data from the ARC 3.5m Telescope’s KOSMOS (Kitt Peak Ohio State Multi-Object Spectrograph) instrument. Built on top of the astro-pyvista package, the pipeline provides a graphical user interface (GUI) to guide users from raw telescope observations to final, science-ready spectra.
My work in astronomy research pushed me toward careful computational work and reproducible analysis. I realized I enjoy building technical tools that other people can actually use. This pipeline is a direct reflection of that interest: it is specifically designed to be accessible for undergraduate students and first-time researchers, minimizing the coding barrier to entry while maintaining rigorous scientific standards.

Built on top of the astro-pyvista package, the pipeline provides a graphical user interface (GUI) to guide users from raw telescope observations to final, science-ready spectra.
My work in astronomy research pushed me toward careful computational work and reproducible analysis. I realized I enjoy building technical tools that other people can actually use. This pipeline is a direct reflection of that interest: it is specifically designed to be accessible for undergraduate students and first-time researchers, minimizing the coding barrier to entry while maintaining rigorous scientific standards.

title: KOSMOS Multi-Slit Data Reduction Pipeline
text:
Why this project matters
Raw astronomical images are rarely perfect. They contain instrumental signatures like readout noise, thermal noise, hot pixels, and uneven illumination. In multi-slit spectroscopy, where light from multiple celestial objects is dispersed across a single detector simultaneously, mapping and extracting clean data becomes a complex geometric and computational challenge.
Standard reduction workflows often require users to navigate sequence-heavy scripts that can be unforgiving of errors. I designed this pipeline around an interactive, tabbed GUI that follows the logical flow of a reduction while allowing the flexibility to move back and forth between steps without breaking the workflow.

title: KOSMOS Multi-Slit Data Reduction Pipeline
text:
Pipeline workflow and architecture
The interface is divided into functional tabs that handle distinct stages of the reduction process.

Calibration
The first step in correcting instrumental signatures is generating master calibration frames. The pipeline automates the combination of:
Biases: To correct for the camera’s preset offset voltage.
Darks: To remove thermal noise and hot pixels using sigma-clipping.
Flats: To correct for dust and uneven illumination along the optical path.
Arcs: To combine neon calibration lamp exposures.


Slit tracing and target mapping
Before extracting data, the software must locate the physical slits on the detector. The pipeline takes a well-exposed flat frame to trace the slit edges automatically based on a user-defined edge threshold. It then cross-references these physical locations with the .kms slit mask file, linking each geometrical slit to its intended astronomical target. Users can dynamically filter this list to reduce only specific targets of interest.


Wavelength calibration
This is one of the most critical steps in the reduction. The pipeline extracts a 2D arc spectrum for each slit and writes the initial mask coordinates into the FITS header to serve as a baseline guess.
The user is then presented with an interactive plot to identify known emission lines and fit a 3rd-degree polynomial to determine the precise pixel-to-wavelength mathematical relationship. Outliers can be removed interactively to bring the RMS below an acceptable threshold before the solution is saved.


Science reduction and extraction
Once the geometry and wavelength solutions are established, the pipeline moves to the science frames. Cosmic Ray Rejection: Applies the lacosmic algorithm to clean the 2D frame of cosmic rays before extraction. 2D Extraction: Extracts individual “slitlets,” applying the master flat correction on a precise slit-by-slit basis to avoid introducing noise from outside the spectral regions. Skyline Fitting: Analyzes rows designated as sky background to identify night sky emission lines, computing subtle, final corrections to the wavelength solution. 1D Extraction: Collapses the 2D slitlet into a final 1D spectrum (flux versus wavelength) by tracing the object, summing the flux, and subtracting the calculated sky background.

title: KOSMOS Multi-Slit Data Reduction Pipeline
text:
Post-processing and analysis
The pipeline includes built-in tools for post-processing the extracted 1D spectra.

Spectra stacking
For targets with multiple exposures, the pipeline provides a stacking interface. This allows users to combine multiple 1D spectra to increase the signal-to-noise ratio, averaging out random noise while preserving the true astronomical signal.


Radial velocity analysis
The AstroAnalysis class provides a secondary GUI specifically for measuring a star’s radial velocity (RV). It automates the fitting of the Calcium II Triplet (CaT) absorption lines at rest wavelengths of 8498.02, 8542.09, and 8662.14 Å. Users can fit a Gaussian or Voigt profile to the lines and log the data. The software calculates the mean RV across the triplet and automatically applies barycentric corrections using astropy to account for the Earth’s motion.

title: KOSMOS Multi-Slit Data Reduction Pipeline
text:
Validation
To ensure the pipeline produces scientifically valid results, I tested it using observational data from an M3 mask. We successfully extracted the spectra, computed the radial velocities, and compared our calculated, barycentric-corrected RVs against established, publicly available values from the APOGEE survey catalog.

title: Life’s Journey
text:
I grew up in a hierarchical society where decisions were traditionally made by my father, my uncles, and other elders; I was far down that line and never expected to make major decisions about my life or anyone else’s. From 2006 to 2016, I lived in Kerr Sering, The Gambia, where I completed a long apprenticeship as an automotive mechanic, learning to rebuild engines and diagnose complex vehicle issues.
In 2016, I moved to Palermo, Italy, where I spent two years apprenticing as a plumber, construction painter, and building electrician.

title: Life’s Journey
text:
A Turning Point in Italy
When I was eighteen years old in Italy, I experienced a profound shift. A woman approached me with government documents and told me I needed to sign them because I was now an adult. I had no idea what they contained, but in that moment, I felt a surge of power mixed with a powerful fear. I realized that with a single stroke of a pen, I could alter or even destroy my life. It was a novel and unsettling feeling that marked the beginning of my independence.

title: Life’s Journey
text:
Discovering the Liberal Arts
After earning my IB Diploma at the United World College Adriatic in Italy, I transitioned to The College of Idaho. On the first day of my Civilization class, Dr. Snyder-Reinke taught us that the liberal arts teach human beings how to be free. I placed that idea at the forefront of everything I do in college. I vowed to learn for the sake of learning—not just to satisfy a syllabus or chase a grade. If I truly understand a topic, I should be able to answer any question posed about it; if I cannot, it is back to the drawing board.
This approach has transformed my worldview. For instance, I used to scoff at the American taboo of discussing politics at the dinner table. However, after studying the American Civil War and learning the tragic, complex social dynamics of American history, I now understand why people avoid it, and I advise against it myself. I may not have received the highest grade in that class, but I received exactly what I needed from it: a deeper understanding of society.

title: Life’s Journey
text:
The Pursuit of Depth
My motivation to pursue graduate school crystallized during my summer 2023 physics research. My teammate and I were working when Dr. Jim Dull stopped by to say hello. We ended up talking for half an hour entirely about units of measurement—centimeters, meters, miles, and furlongs. It was one of the best conversations of my life. Afterward, I realized there was no topic in the world I could speak about with that same incredible depth of understanding. I knew then that an undergraduate degree would not be enough; I needed to attend graduate school.
That realization also brought a moment of painful humility. I remembered that as a freshman, out of pure ignorance, I had laughed at a communication professor and told him I didn’t need his class. Realizing how incredibly difficult it is just to survive an undergraduate semester, let alone earn a doctoral degree, I wept at the thought that I had insulted a man’s hard work, sweat, and tears. Since that day, I have vowed never again to speak ignorantly about something I do not understand.

title: Life’s Journey
text:
Looking Forward
As I look past graduation, my primary goal (Plan A) is to attend graduate school to achieve the depth of knowledge I deeply admire in my mentors. My immediate secondary goal (Plan B) is securing a role in industry that will allow me to support myself and maintain my residency in the United States post-graduation.

title: Statement
text:
This page is adapted from the personal statement uploaded with this portfolio starter. It works well as a statement page for the BSU computational PhD application context and can also serve as a deeper motivation page on the portfolio site. The linked PDF is your original uploaded file.

Download statement PDF



My long-term goal is to build robots that are actually suited to the needs of the communities I care about. That goal begins with understanding the systems those machines depend on, including the computational and physical foundations behind semiconductor devices and control systems.
I grew up in Tambasansang, a small farming village in The Gambia. My early fascination with machines began through hands-on work around engines and electronics. Later, studying physics and mathematics gave me a deeper way to understand those systems instead of only using them.



At The College of Idaho, I worked in astronomy research and software-centered scientific workflows. That experience pushed me toward careful computational work, reproducible analysis, and the experimental side of physics. It also showed me how much I enjoy building technical tools that other people can actually use.



My interest in robotics is practical. I want to build affordable tools that reduce physical burden and expand opportunity in communities where cost and context matter. I can teach myself a great deal about prototyping, programming, and system integration, but I also want deeper formal training in the modeling and simulation tools needed to move from system-level design to a stronger understanding of the underlying components.



A computational PhD path fits because I want stronger preparation in computational modeling, simulation, and scientific problem solving. That training would help me connect robotics, physical systems, and the deeper design logic behind technologies that must work under real constraints rather than ideal ones.

title: Customer Churn Modeling with Reproducible Machine Learning
text:
Exploratory data analysis
A good report does not flood the page with charts. The purpose here is to identify a few patterns that matter for modeling and interpretation.



























Three patterns stand out. First, churn is present but not dominant, so the problem is somewhat imbalanced without being extreme. Second, contract type appears strongly related to churn. Third, churn risk is not likely to be captured by a single numeric variable alone, which supports using a preprocessing pipeline that handles mixed data types.

title: Customer Churn Modeling with Reproducible Machine Learning
text:
Feature engineering and preprocessing
The dataset includes both numeric and categorical variables. A clean way to handle this is a column transformer inside a pipeline.


Show code
X = churn.drop(columns="Churn")
y = churn["Churn"]

numeric_features = X.select_dtypes(include=["number"]).columns.tolist()
categorical_features = X.select_dtypes(exclude=["number"]).columns.tolist()

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.30,
    random_state=4025,
    stratify=y,
)

numeric_preprocess = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ]
)

categorical_preprocess = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
        ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
    ]
)

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("num", numeric_preprocess, numeric_features),
        ("cat", categorical_preprocess, categorical_features),
    ]
)

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=4025)

title: Customer Churn Modeling with Reproducible Machine Learning
text:
Modeling
A good portfolio report should compare a simple, interpretable baseline with at least one stronger nonlinear model.


Show code
logistic_model = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("preprocess", preprocessor),
        ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)),
    ]
)

forest_model = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("preprocess", preprocessor),
        ("model", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=400,
            min_samples_leaf=5,
            random_state=4025,
        )),
    ]
)




Show code
scoring = {
    "roc_auc": "roc_auc",
    "accuracy": "accuracy",
    "precision": "precision",
    "recall": "recall",
}

cv_results = []

for name, model in {
    "Logistic Regression": logistic_model,
    "Random Forest": forest_model,
}.items():
    scores = cross_validate(
        model,
        X_train,
        y_train,
        cv=cv,
        scoring=scoring,
        n_jobs=-1,
        return_train_score=False,
    )
    cv_results.append({
        "model": name,
        "cv_roc_auc_mean": scores["test_roc_auc"].mean(),
        "cv_accuracy_mean": scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
        "cv_precision_mean": scores["test_precision"].mean(),
        "cv_recall_mean": scores["test_recall"].mean(),
    })

cv_df = pd.DataFrame(cv_results).sort_values("cv_roc_auc_mean", ascending=False)

title: Customer Churn Modeling with Reproducible Machine Learning
text:
Test-set performance


Show code
best_model = logistic_model
best_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_prob = best_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
y_pred = (y_prob >= 0.50).astype(int)

test_metrics = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "metric": ["ROC-AUC", "Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall"],
        "value": [
            roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob),
            accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),
            precision_score(y_test, y_pred),
            recall_score(y_test, y_pred),
        ],
    }
)

The exact best model may change after tuning, but this structure already supports a professional discussion. Logistic regression is often a strong baseline in churn work because it is interpretable and stable. A tree-based model is useful to check whether nonlinear interactions meaningfully improve ranking performance.

title: Customer Churn Modeling with Reproducible Machine Learning
text:
Performance analysis
For a professional writeup, this section should move past metric reporting and explain tradeoffs.

ROC-AUC tells us how well the model separates higher-risk from lower-risk customers across thresholds.
Precision matters when retention outreach is expensive and false alarms are costly.
Recall matters when missing a likely churner is costly.
Threshold choice should depend on business constraints rather than habit.

A natural next step would be to compare several decision thresholds and frame the tradeoff in operational terms.

title: Customer Churn Modeling with Reproducible Machine Learning
text:
Conclusion
This project shows a complete and readable classification workflow:

start with a clear prediction question,
perform targeted exploratory analysis,
build a preprocessing pipeline for mixed data,
compare models with cross-validation,
evaluate test-set performance with ROC-AUC and threshold-aware metrics,
close with decision-oriented interpretation rather than code commentary.

For a stronger final version, I would add modest hyperparameter tuning, feature importance or coefficient interpretation, and a short section on limitations such as missing behavioral variables or possible temporal leakage concerns.

Download statement PDF



My long-term goal is to build robots that are actually suited to the needs of the communities I care about. That goal begins with understanding the systems those machines depend on, including the computational and physical foundations behind semiconductor devices and control systems.
I grew up in Tambasansang, a small farming village in The Gambia. My early fascination with machines began through hands-on work around engines and electronics. Later, studying physics and mathematics gave me a deeper way to understand those systems instead of only using them.



At The College of Idaho, I worked in astronomy research and software-centered scientific workflows. That experience pushed me toward careful computational work, reproducible analysis, and the experimental side of physics. It also showed me how much I enjoy building technical tools that other people can actually use.



My interest in robotics is practical. I want to build affordable tools that reduce physical burden and expand opportunity in communities where cost and context matter. I can teach myself a great deal about prototyping, programming, and system integration, but I also want deeper formal training in the modeling and simulation tools needed to move from system-level design to a stronger understanding of the underlying components.



A computational PhD path fits because I want stronger preparation in computational modeling, simulation, and scientific problem solving. That training would help me connect robotics, physical systems, and the deeper design logic behind technologies that must work under real constraints rather than ideal ones.

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
AgriBot-Assist is a low-cost, solar-powered farming robot designed for small agricultural plots. The project is aimed at reducing the physical burden of plowing and related field work for low-income farming families who do not have access to expensive modern equipment. The current concept combines a Raspberry Pi, Arduino controllers, LoRa communication, GPS, solar power, and onboard sensing to create a practical autonomous field assistant. :contentReferenceoaicite:0
What makes this project important to me is that it grows out of a real problem I know personally. In my personal statement, I explain that I grew up in a farming village where hard physical labor shaped daily life, and where affordable agricultural automation could create more room for education, creativity, and long-term community growth. That motivation is the reason this project exists. :contentReferenceoaicite:1

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
Why this project matters
Many smallholder farmers still rely on manual labor and animal traction because tractors and other modern machines are too expensive. The proposal frames that problem in practical terms: physical strain, time loss, limited efficiency, and the way economic pressure can pull children into farm labor instead of school. AgriBot-Assist is meant to address one part of that problem by automating plowing on small plots with a design built around affordability and accessible parts. :contentReferenceoaicite:2
The larger goal is not just to build a robot that moves. It is to design a system that can work under the constraints that matter in the real world: limited budgets, off-grid power, simple interfaces, and field boundaries that are not already digitized. The proposal sets that goal clearly as a functional prototype that can autonomously plow within GPS-defined small farm boundaries. :contentReferenceoaicite:3

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
Project goals
The current project goals are:

finalize a low-cost mechanical and electronic design
build and integrate the prototype chassis, drive system, plow mechanism, solar power system, and control electronics
develop Raspberry Pi software for boundary calculation, interface logic, and communication
develop Arduino software for navigation, motor control, obstacle avoidance, and plowing logic
test the robot in controlled field-like conditions
document the build, code, and performance of the prototype

These goals come directly from the proposal and give the project a clear engineering path rather than leaving it as a broad idea. :contentReferenceoaicite:4

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
System architecture
The robot is designed around a split-control architecture.

Raspberry Pi responsibilities
The Raspberry Pi acts as the central brain. It is intended to handle:

GPS parsing
boundary creation from coordinate points
path planning
task coordination
obstacle avoidance
communication with the Arduino Mega through serial
user interface logic

The design notes explicitly state that the Pi should receive farm boundary points, convert them into a polygon, select a starting point, compute the path, and send movement or task commands to the Arduino Mega. :contentReferenceoaicite:5


Arduino responsibilities
The Arduino Mega is responsible for the real-time control layer. Its main role is to receive commands from the Pi and drive the wheel motors and the plowing motor through motor drivers. This separation keeps timing-critical hardware control on the microcontroller while leaving higher-level planning on the Pi. :contentReferenceoaicite:6


Boundary definition and communication
The communication plan uses LoRa and GPS in stages:

A GPS and LoRa pair connected to an Arduino Uno collects coordinate points.
Those coordinates are sent to the Raspberry Pi.
The Pi builds the polygonal boundary of the farm.
A starting point is selected.
The Pi sends guidance and control information to the Arduino Mega.
The Mega drives the motors while the Pi handles navigation logic and task coordination.

The current design also notes that LoRa communication is not yet fully working, so the code should be written in a way that preserves LoRa support for later while still allowing test runs with the built-in GPS system. :contentReferenceoaicite:7

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
Hardware stack
The current hardware plan includes:

Raspberry Pi 5 with Raspberry Pi OS and NVMe storage
Arduino Uno
Arduino Mega
2 LoRa modules
2 NEO-6M GPS modules
RCWL-1601 ultrasonic sensor
MG995 servo motor for ultrasonic scanning
MPU-6050 gyroscope / accelerometer
4 geared DC wheel motors with encoders
BTS7960 motor drivers
1 geared motor for raising and lowering the plowing tool
12V lithium-ion battery packs

The hardware notes also specify that the wheel motors use encoders and that each major motor function is paired with its own motor driver. :contentReferenceoaicite:8

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
Navigation and path-planning idea
One of the more interesting parts of the design is the idea of treating the farm boundary like a 3D printer bed. The notes describe the polygonal field boundary as the equivalent of a print area, with the robot moving through it like a print head or extruder assembly. In that model, the Pi computes the full path before the plowing action begins, taking into account the dimensions of the robot and attached tool. :contentReferenceoaicite:9
That is a strong way to explain the project because it turns the navigation problem into something concrete and intuitive. It also highlights that this is not just a remote-control rover. It is meant to be a task-oriented machine with planned coverage over a defined working area.

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
Interface and GUI roadmap
The GUI roadmap shows a clear intention to make the interface more usable and more visual over time. The sketch includes:

coordinate entry fields
buttons for adding and removing points
a path planning area
save and load path controls
a starting point input
action buttons for send path and start, pause, resume, and stop
a connect Arduino control
graphical logging instead of plain text
progress and time statistics
sensor readouts displayed as graphs rather than single values

That roadmap is useful because it shows that the interface is being treated as part of the engineering problem, not just as a last-minute add-on. :contentReferenceoaicite:10

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
Current development status
At this stage, the project is best described as an active prototype and system design effort rather than a finished field robot.
What is already clear: - the mission and use case - the hardware stack - the split between Pi logic and Arduino control - the communication plan - the path-planning concept - the intended user interface
What is still in progress: - reliable LoRa communication between the Arduino Uno and the Pi - full system integration - field testing of autonomous motion inside the defined boundary - plowing validation - final GUI implementation - performance documentation
The proposal also defines concrete yes/no testing goals: whether the robot can receive coordinates, map them on the monitor, move within the boundaries, and till the land in a test environment. :contentReferenceoaicite:11

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
Expected impact
The long-term goal is to reduce physical strain, save time, support education by reducing child labor pressure, improve farming efficiency, and promote renewable energy use in agriculture. The project is also meant to be a step toward locally meaningful technology, not just a copy of equipment built for a different environment and different economic conditions. :contentReferenceoaicite:12 :contentReferenceoaicite:13
That broader context matters. AgriBot-Assist is not just a robotics exercise. It is a design response to a real constraint: how to build agricultural technology that is actually realistic for the communities it is meant to serve.

title: AgriBot-Assist
text:
Technical focus
This project lets me work across several technical areas at once:

embedded systems
robotics
Python-based coordination and interface design
microcontroller programming
serial and LoRa communication
GPS-based path planning
obstacle avoidance
prototyping and hardware integration

It also reflects the hands-on direction I describe in my broader work and academic trajectory: building systems that connect software, hardware, and real-world constraints. :contentReferenceoaicite:14 :contentReferenceoaicite:15
